title: Review 77: Unlocking Student Potential
author: Chris Jones
summary: Chris Jones, drawing on more than four decades in education and work with hundreds of schools, argues that pupil motivation is a product of system design and not a trait to be fixed in the child. He applies autonomy, mastery and purpose as lenses on curriculum, timetabling and relationships, and shows how schools that praise pupil voice can still prescribe every minute of the timetable. He suggests propensity tools such as the GC Index can help teachers align group roles with how pupils naturally contribute, moving the conversation from fixed labels to contribution. Curriculum coherence and the timetable are presented as underused strategic levers, and culture is defined as the lived experience of children lesson by lesson. His practical advice is to stop asking how to motivate pupils and ask how the experience of learning has been designed, aligning curriculum, time, relationships and leadership decisions so that motivation emerges instead of being generated.
points: Motivation is better treated as a diagnostic of the school system than as an individual trait, so disengagement should prompt the question of what the system is telling us.

Autonomy, mastery and purpose give schools three practical levers: ownership within the curriculum, visible success through scaffolding and timely feedback, and relationships that make pupils feel known.
Intentions such as pupil voice fail when timetable and curriculum structure leave no real room for choice.
Propensity tools like the GC Index can help assign group roles that match how pupils add value, shifting from labels to contribution.
Timetable decisions such as lesson length or when an enjoyed subject falls can change attendance and engagement and deserve strategic attention.
quotes: Put simply, pupils are not motivated or unmotivated in isolation. They are responding to the experience of the system we have designed around them.

Yet when we looked at the timetable and curriculum structure, there was very little space for choice or exploration. Everything was tightly prescribed. The intention was there. The design was not aligned.
If pupils are disengaged, it is rarely helpful to ask what is wrong with the pupils. The more powerful question is: what is the system telling us?
What changes is not just the outcome, but the experience. Pupils begin to see themselves as having a meaningful contribution.
And yet, too often, the timetable is treated as a logistical exercise rather than a strategic one.
And culture, as I often say, is simply the lived experience of children. It is what happens lesson by lesson, day by day, over time.
Adding more interventions, more monitoring, or more accountability may create short-term change, but it rarely leads to sustained improvement.
